solution:
Each allowed move sends every corner to a neighboring corner. This restricts the configuration after \(19\) moves enough that the final move is forced.

The corner positions split into the two opposite pairs
\[
\{(1,1),(-1,-1)\},\qquad
\{(-1,1),(1,-1)\}.
\]
Every allowed move switches these pairs. Since \(19\) is odd, vertex \(A\) must then be at either \((-1,1)\) or \((1,-1)\).

For either location of \(A\), vertex \(B\) has two possible neighboring locations. Rotations and reflections preserve opposite vertices, so once \(A\) and \(B\) are placed, \(C\) must be opposite \(A\) and \(D\) opposite \(B\). There are therefore at most four possible complete configurations after \(19\) moves.

Applying \(L,R,H,V\) once produces four distinct configurations of exactly this kind. Thus any sequence of \(19\) moves has the same overall effect as one of \(L,R,H,V\). Each has a unique inverse among the allowed moves: \(L\) and \(R\) undo each other, while \(H\) and \(V\) each undo themselves.

We may therefore choose the first \(19\) moves freely, then append exactly one move that restores every label. Different prefixes give different full sequences, and every successful sequence arises this way. The number is
\[
4^{19}=\boxed{2^{38}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Grouping the moves into pairs reduces the problem to four possible overall effects. We can count how many sequences reach each effect after each pair.

Define the following coordinate rules:
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(x,y)&=(x,y),&T(x,y)&=(-x,-y),\\
F(x,y)&=(y,x),&G(x,y)&=(-y,-x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(I\) leaves every label in place, \(T\) is a half-turn, and \(F,G\) are reflections across the two diagonal lines.

The table lists the effect of each ordered pair of allowed moves. Apply the row move first, then the column move. For example, \(L\) followed by \(H\) sends \((x,y)\) to \((-y,x)\) and then to \((-y,-x)\), giving \(G\).

| First move | Then \(L\) | Then \(R\) | Then \(H\) | Then \(V\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(L\) | \(T\) | \(I\) | \(G\) | \(F\) |
| \(R\) | \(I\) | \(T\) | \(F\) | \(G\) |
| \(H\) | \(F\) | \(G\) | \(I\) | \(T\) |
| \(V\) | \(G\) | \(F\) | \(T\) | \(I\) |

Each effect occurs four times among the \(16\) possible pairs. Also, composing any two of \(I,T,F,G\) gives one of these four effects again, and each effect undoes itself. Consequently, from any current state among these four, exactly four next pairs lead to each target state.

After one pair, there are \(N_1=4\) sequences per state. If there are \(N_j\) sequences per state after \(j\) pairs, then each of the four current states contributes \(4N_j\) sequences to a fixed target state. Thus the counts stay equal and satisfy
\[
N_{j+1}=16N_j.
\]
Twenty moves make ten pairs, so the number ending at \(I\) is
\[
N_{10}=4\cdot16^9=\boxed{2^{38}}.
\]
Every sequence has a unique division into these consecutive pairs, so none are omitted or counted twice. The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Count two moves at a time
